desc: survivesVerification used filter(Boolean), so a truthy-malformed vote ({} / {real:null}) stayed in the denominator as a refutation and could silently drop a real blocker — the guard failed OPEN on invalid input instead of closed

buildgate classified with `=== 'mutating'` (narrow allowlist) while the rails path fail-closed-CHECKS any unrecognized 'other' structured tool — a secondary gate covered a NARROWER input surface than the primary gate it shadows, so a novel mutator name bypassed it

mergeHooks used (hooks.event ?? []).filter — ?? defaults only null/undefined, so a valid-JSON but non-array event value (object/string/number) threw an uncaught TypeError and crashed the scaffolder

isAdlcHook used an unanchored substring regex, so a user hook whose command merely CONTAINED an adlc basename (run-adlc-audit.mjs) was misclassified as ours and silently dropped — an identity match not anchored to a boundary destroyed user data

the doc honesty smoke asserted a required string is PRESENT but not that a contradictory overclaim is ABSENT, so a future edit could keep 'buildgate is advisory' and add 'the in-session hook is unbypassable' and still pass — presence-only checks don't enforce honesty

changedFiles and gitDiff scan git output without -z or quotepath disabled, so non-ASCII paths are C-quoted and the returned string is not the authoritative path a scanner needs.
rail-freeze checkRailEdits consumes the quoted non-authoritative changed-file list, so editing a frozen rail path with a non-ASCII filename is never matched and the gate passes silently.
spec-lint heading and criteria scanning has no fenced-code awareness, so a heading-like line inside an example fence desyncs section state and real acceptance criteria are silently dropped.
the read-only shell classifier is anchored at start but not end, so a whitelisted read verb chained before a mutating command via semicolon lets a rail write evade the enforcing gate.

the shell mutation allowlist omits network-fetch-to-file tools and the reactive git-diff backstop is blind to gitignored trust-root files, allowing a fetch to overwrite the active-ticket trust root undetected.

the surface-intersection changed-files derivation requires literal a/ and b/ diff prefixes, so an adversarial diff using alternate apply-compatible prefixes is classified out of scope and the fuzzer skips an in-surface mutation.
the documented bare file_path fallback does not exist, so a write target under an unrecognized container shape is invisible to scope-violation detection rather than conservatively surfaced.

When a CLI advisory check gains a new mode flag, sibling copies of the same check embedded in other plugins or integrations (e.g. multiple editor Stop-hook implementations that each independently shell out to the same underlying command) are easy to miss; a repo-wide grep for the exact shelled-out command is needed to find every caller, not just the ones the ticket scope happened to name.

Tightening a shared library function's tolerance semantics (moving from an unscoped 'anywhere' tolerance to a scoped positional tolerance) silently changes behavior for every existing caller of that function, not just the caller the change was written for; each existing call site needs its own comment update and its own regression test for the new boundary condition, or the behavior change ships unreviewed and untested at those sites.

A new CLI flag that is unit-tested only against the underlying library function in isolation has no coverage for the actual argument-parsing and flag-to-option wiring in the binary; a flipped negation, a typo in the flag name, or a dropped option pass-through would ship undetected unless a test spawns the real binary end to end.

An advisory session-end hook that reports a security-relevant signal (evidence-chain tamper detection) is often the actual bug being fixed by a change, yet has no direct test coverage of its own; downstream test files assert only on a stubbed spawn's canned return value, never on the literal arguments passed to the spawn, so a reverted fix would leave every existing test green.

A chain-only (unkeyed hash-linkage) integrity check cannot distinguish a wholesale-forged, entirely-unsigned ledger from an honest ledger whose real history genuinely predates a security feature's adoption, because the forging operation requires no secret; when a lenient/tolerant mode is extended to a new caller that treats a clean chain-only pass as a tamper-detection signal, that caller inherits this limitation even if the underlying function's guarantee was previously only relied on by callers with an independent defense-in-depth check. The limitation should be documented explicitly wherever the lenient mode is offered, not left implicit.
